stimuli.title: From a short story: The Repair Shop
stimuli.text:
The bell over the door still worked. Nadia had expected that, somehow, everything in her father's shop would have stopped when he did: the clocks, the bell, the little fan he kept pointed at the workbench. Instead the wall clocks went on ticking out of step with one another, a crowd of small, stubborn voices.

She had come to sign the papers and hand over the keys. The buyer wanted the space for a phone store. "Clean it out by Friday," the agent had said, as if forty years could be swept into a bin.

On the bench lay a pocket watch with its back open, a paper tag tied to the chain. In her father's square handwriting: *Mrs. Okafor. Mainspring. Promised for the 14th.* The 14th was tomorrow.

Nadia sat down on his stool. It was too low for her, and she did not raise it. She found the loupe in the drawer where it had always been and fitted it to her eye the way he had shown her when she was nine and bored and wanted only to go home. The tiny gears swam, then held still.

She worked until the streetlights came on. Twice she nearly gave up; twice she heard, as clearly as if he were leaning over her shoulder, his one piece of advice: *Slow is fast.* When the watch finally began to tick, she laughed out loud in the empty shop.

In the morning she called the agent. Friday, she told him, was not going to work after all.

stimuli.title: Night Route (a poem)
stimuli.text:
At four the bus is mostly light and hum,

a lit room rolling through a sleeping town.

The driver knows each rider by the stop:

the baker at Ninth Street, flour on her sleeve,

the nurse who boards at Grand with tired eyes,

the boy with schoolbooks who should be asleep.

They do not speak. They do not need to speak.

He holds the doors a second past the rule

for anyone who runs. That is his gift,

the only one he has to give: a second,

a small, warm room that waits for them, and goes.

stimuli.title: Why Cities Are Planting Shade
stimuli.text:
On a summer afternoon, a downtown parking lot can be many degrees hotter than a park a few blocks away. Scientists call this difference the urban heat island effect. Asphalt, concrete and dark roofs absorb sunlight all day and release that heat slowly, so cities stay warm long after sunset.

Trees work against this in two ways. Their leaves block sunlight before it reaches the pavement, and they release water vapor through tiny openings in their leaves, which cools the air around them in much the same way that sweat cools skin. A street lined with mature trees can feel noticeably cooler to a person walking beneath them.

For this reason, a number of cities have set goals for tree canopy, the share of the city's land covered by leaves when seen from above. Planting is the easy part. A young tree in a narrow sidewalk pit needs water for its first few summers, and many die before they are large enough to cast real shade. Cities that succeed tend to pair planting with a plan for watering and care.

Canopy is also uneven. In many cities, wealthier neighborhoods have far more tree cover than poorer ones, which means the residents least able to afford air conditioning often live on the hottest streets. Some planners now map heat and canopy together and plant first where the gap is widest.

stimuli.title: Editorial: Keep the Library Open Late
stimuli.text:
The town council will vote next month on whether to end the library's evening hours to save money. That would be a mistake, and the council should reject it.

The library stays open until 9 p.m. three nights a week. Those are the only hours many working residents can use it. The council's own figures show that evening visits make up nearly a third of all visits, even though the evening hours are less than a fifth of the hours the library is open. In other words, the evenings are the library's busiest time, not its quietest.

Who comes at night? Parents who pick up children after work. Adults taking online classes who need a quiet table and a reliable connection. People applying for jobs who do not own a printer. Cutting the evening hours would not hurt everyone equally; it would hurt the residents with the fewest other options.

The savings, meanwhile, are small: about one percent of the town budget, according to the finance office. There are better places to find that money. The council should keep the doors open, and the lights on.

stimuli.title: The Canal That Moved a Nation
stimuli.text:
In 1817, work began on a channel to connect the Hudson River to Lake Erie across upstate New York. Many people thought the plan was foolish; critics nicknamed it "Clinton's Ditch" after Governor DeWitt Clinton, who championed it. When the Erie Canal opened in 1825, it stretched about 363 miles from Albany to Buffalo.

Before the canal, moving goods from the Great Lakes region to the East Coast meant slow, costly travel by wagon over rough roads. Canal boats, pulled by mules walking along a towpath, could carry far heavier loads for a fraction of the price. Shipping costs fell sharply, and farm products from the West began flowing east while manufactured goods flowed west.

The effects reached well beyond trade. New York City, at the mouth of the Hudson, became the nation's leading port. Towns such as Syracuse and Rochester grew along the route. Settlers used the canal to move into the Great Lakes states, speeding the growth of the Midwest.

Railroads eventually carried most of the freight the canal once handled, but the canal's success had already shown that a bold public project could reshape the economy of an entire region.

stimuli.title: From a short story: Counter Shift
stimuli.text:
Marisol had worked the counter at the Blue Plate for three weeks before her grandmother came in.

She saw her through the window first, small and straight-backed, clutching her purse with both hands as though the sidewalk might take it. Abuela never ate in restaurants. "Why pay someone," she liked to say, "to cook worse than you?"

She took the stool at the end and studied the menu for a long time. Marisol poured her coffee and waited, suddenly aware of the grease spot on her apron and the way her ponytail had come loose.

"The eggs," Abuela said at last. "Over easy. And the toast."

Marisol carried the order back to Lou at the grill and stood watching him crack the eggs, as if she could make them come out right by staring. When she set the plate down, Abuela tasted the eggs, chewed slowly, and said nothing at all.

She left a tip under the saucer, folded into a small square. Later, when the lunch crowd had thinned, Marisol unfolded it. It was a five-dollar bill, and inside it a note on the back of a receipt, in careful capital letters: THE EGGS WERE NOT BAD. YOU STOOD UP STRAIGHT.

Marisol read it twice, then tucked it into her apron pocket, where it stayed for the rest of the summer.

stimuli.title: February Garden (a poem)
stimuli.text:
My mother walks the garden in her boots

where nothing grows, and names what isn't there:

the beans along the fence, the squash, the roots

of onions sleeping under frozen air.

I see a field of mud and broken stalks.

She sees July, and reads it like a map,

and counts the rows in footsteps as she walks,

the seed packets rustling in her lap

each night beside the stove. I used to laugh.

Now I am learning how she reads the ground,

how hope is just a kind of careful math,

how what is buried is not what is drowned.

stimuli.title: The Return of the Bald Eagle
stimuli.text:
By the early 1960s, the bald eagle, the national bird of the United States, was in serious trouble. Fewer than 500 nesting pairs remained in the lower 48 states. Hunting and the loss of nesting trees had played a part, but scientists eventually identified a less obvious cause: the pesticide DDT.

DDT was sprayed widely to kill insects. It washed into rivers and lakes, where it built up in fish, and eagles that ate the fish absorbed it. The chemical did not usually kill adult birds. Instead, it caused them to lay eggs with shells so thin that they cracked when the parents sat on them. Year after year, nests produced few or no chicks.

In 1972, the United States banned most uses of DDT. Eagles were also protected under federal law, and biologists raised chicks and released them in areas where eagles had disappeared. The recovery was slow at first, then dramatic. By 2007, the population had grown so much that the bald eagle was removed from the list of endangered and threatened species.

The eagle's comeback is often cited as proof that careful science and firm policy can reverse damage to wildlife. It is also a reminder that the harm a chemical does may show up far from where it was used.

stimuli.title: Letter to patients: Riverside Health Center
stimuli.text:
Dear Patients,

Starting March 3, Riverside Health Center will change its hours to better fit your schedules. We will open at 7 a.m. instead of 8 a.m. on weekdays, and we will add Saturday hours from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. To make this possible, we will close at 5 p.m. on Fridays instead of 7 p.m.

These changes come from you. Last fall, more than 600 patients answered our survey, and the most common request was for appointments before work. Many also asked for a weekend option for children's checkups.

Walk-in visits will still be available every weekday morning, but we strongly encourage you to book ahead, especially for Saturday, which we expect to fill quickly. You can book through the patient portal or by calling the front desk.

If an early or weekend time would help a family member who does not use the portal, please let them know about the change.

Thank you for helping us serve you better.

The Riverside Health Center Team

stimuli.title: Two views on the four-day school week
stimuli.text:
**Passage 1** (from a parent's letter to a school board)

When our district moved to a four-day week, I worried. Two years later, I am a convert. The longer school days were hard at first, but my children now have a full day each week for medical appointments, family time and catching up. The district saved money on buses and heating, and it has had an easier time hiring teachers, who see the schedule as a benefit. Attendance on school days has improved, because fewer families pull children out for appointments.

**Passage 2** (from an education researcher's article)

The four-day week is popular with many families and teachers, and districts report modest savings. But the evidence on learning is mixed. Some studies have found small declines in test scores, especially where the extra day is not used for anything structured. The schedule can also be hard on working parents who must find or pay for care on the fifth day, and on students who rely on school meals. Before switching, a district should ask what the fifth day will be for, and who will be left without support on it.

stimuli.title: From a short story: The Keeper's Daughter
stimuli.text:
Every night for eleven years, Ellen's father had climbed the hundred and four steps of the lighthouse to light the lamp. Every night for eleven years, Ellen had counted them with him, first from his arms, then from his hand, then a step ahead, impatient.

Now he lay in bed with a fever, and the storm was coming in from the east, black and low over the water.

"I can do it," she said.

He looked at her for a long moment, the way he looked at the sky before deciding whether the fishing boats should go out. Then he nodded once.

The wind pushed against the tower like a shoulder against a door. Halfway up, the lantern in her hand guttered, and she stood still in the dark, listening to the sea throw itself at the rocks below. She thought of the boats out there, of the men who had nodded to her in the harbor, of their wives waiting at kitchen windows. She climbed.

When the great lamp caught and the beam swung out over the water, she pressed her forehead against the cold glass and let herself breathe. Far off, a single light answered, and then another, turning toward home.

stimuli.title: Why Bridges Have Gaps
stimuli.text:
Drive across a long bridge and you may feel a small bump every so often, where a metal strip with teeth like a comb crosses the road. These strips are expansion joints, and without them many bridges would tear themselves apart.

Almost all materials expand when they warm up and contract when they cool down. Steel and concrete are no exception. The change in a single foot of steel is tiny, but a bridge deck may be hundreds or thousands of feet long, and over a year it may face temperatures from well below freezing to the heat of a summer afternoon in direct sun. Across its full length, that adds up to a change of several inches.

If the deck were fixed solidly at both ends, the expanding material would have nowhere to go. It would push against the supports with enormous force, cracking concrete or buckling steel. An expansion joint leaves a gap that can open and close as the deck moves, while the comb-shaped plates let tires roll smoothly over it.

Engineers plan for this movement long before construction begins. Railroad tracks, sidewalks and even some large buildings include similar gaps for the same reason.

stimuli.title: Draft: a personal account, How I Learned to Budget
stimuli.text:
¶1 Two years ago, I had no idea where my paycheck went. I would get paid on Friday, and by the next Thursday I was __lending__ [1] lunch money from my sister. I decided something had to change.

¶2 My first step was simple: for one month, I wrote down every dollar I spent. __The results surprised me, I was spending more on takeout than on groceries.__ [2] Small purchases, a coffee here and a snack there, added up to almost two hundred dollars.

¶3 __Next,__ [3] I made a plan. I divided my pay into three parts: bills, savings and spending money. __I keep the savings in a separate account so I wont__ [4] be tempted to use it. At first, the savings part was only twenty dollars a week. __Twenty dollars a week does not sound like a lot of money to most people who hear about it.__ [5] Still, by the end of the year, I had more than a thousand dollars.

¶4 __My sister also likes to cook.__ [6] The hardest part was saying no to friends who wanted to eat out every weekend. I started inviting them over for potluck dinners instead. To my surprise, __they enjoyed it as much as me.__ [7]

¶5 Budgeting has not made me rich, but it has made me __calmer and less anxious and more relaxed__ [8]. I no longer dread the end of the week. __Having learned to track my spending, my confidence grew.__ [9] __If you are thinking about starting a budget, begin by writing everything down.__ [10]

¶1 Last month, the Eastfield High robotics team __won it's__ [1] first regional championship. The team of twelve students built a robot that could sort recycling by material, a task that took them most of the school year.

¶2 __The project began in September, when the team chose a problem to solve.__ [2] Team captain Ana Reyes said the idea came from the school cafeteria, where bins were often filled with the wrong items. "We wanted to build something useful," she explained, "not just something that __look__ [3] cool."

¶3 Building the robot was harder than __the team expects__ [4]. The first design jammed whenever it picked up a crushed can. __The students rebuilt the gripper four times, testing each version for hours__ [5]. __Their coach, Mr. Dale, who teaches physics, he stayed late__ [6] with them many evenings.

¶4 __Furthermore,__ [7] the hard work paid off. At the competition, judges praised the robot's speed and __the way it was really, really accurate__ [8]. __The team will now go on to compete at the state level of competition in the month of May.__ [9]

¶5 Reyes hopes the robot will one day be used in the cafeteria. "We already know it works," she said. "__Now we just need to convince the principal to let us plug it in.__" [10]

stimuli.title: Draft: a report on a city bike-share program
stimuli.text:
¶1 Two years ago, the city of Brookport launched a bike-share program with 300 bikes at 40 stations. __Riders unlock a bike with a phone app and return it to any station.__ [1]

¶2 __Use has grown steadily.__ [2] In the first year, riders took about 90,000 trips. In the second year, that number __exploded wildly__ [3] to over 150,000. Most trips were short, under three miles.

¶3 __The bikes are painted bright green.__ [4] A survey of riders found that many use the bikes to reach bus and train stops. __For these riders, the bikes fill a gap; the last mile__ [5] between transit and home.

¶4 __However,__ [6] the program faces challenges. Stations in the busiest areas often run out of bikes by morning, while stations near parks sit full. __The city have hired__ [7] staff to move bikes by truck, but this is costly.

¶5 __Each of the stations need more docks__ [8], according to the report. __The report recommends adding twenty stations and using price discounts to encourage riders to return bikes where they are needed.__ [9]

stimuli.title: Draft: a personal account, Learning to Swim at Thirty
stimuli.text:
¶1 I grew up near the ocean, but I never learned to swim. __As a child, I was too scared, as an adult, I was too embarrassed.__ [1] Last summer, at thirty, I finally signed up for lessons.

¶2 __The first lesson was terrifying.__ [2] I clung to the side of the pool while children half my height splashed past. My instructor, a retired lifeguard named Grace, did not rush me. __She taught me to float first, she said__ [3] that a swimmer who can float can always rest.

¶3 __Pools are cleaned with chlorine.__ [4] By the third week, I could swim the width of the pool. By the sixth, I could swim a full length without stopping. __Me and two other adult students__ [5] started meeting early to practice.

¶4 __For example,__ [6] learning to swim taught me more than a skill. It showed me that being a beginner is nothing to be ashamed of, at any age. __It's a lesson that I now try to apply and use for every new thing that I try.__ [7]

¶5 __This summer, I plan to swim in the ocean for the first time.__ [8] __I am excited, and I am a little nervous, and I am ready.__ [9]

questions.stem: Why did Nadia originally come to the shop?
options: To sign papers and hand over the keys
To finish repairing a watch for a customer
To meet the buyer of the building
questions.explanation: The story says she "had come to sign the papers and hand over the keys." Fixing Mrs. Okafor's watch is something she decides to do once she is there.

questions.stem: The narrator describes the ticking wall clocks as "a crowd of small, stubborn voices." This description suggests that the clocks:
options: are too loud for Nadia to think
carry on as if nothing has ended
need to be repaired before the sale
questions.explanation: Nadia expected everything to stop when her father died, but the clocks keep "ticking" anyway. Calling them stubborn shows they go on as though nothing has ended.

questions.stem: Nadia's choice not to raise the height of the stool most likely shows that she:
options: does not plan to stay very long
has never worked at the bench before
wants to keep the shop as her father left it
is too tired after the drive to adjust the seat
questions.explanation: Leaving the stool "too low for her" keeps it the way her father had it, the first sign of how much the shop means to her. She has worked at the bench before, as a child.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Old businesses cannot compete with new ones
Children rarely value the skills their parents teach them
Hard work is always rewarded with money
Carrying on someone's work can keep a bond alive
questions.explanation: Nadia finishes her father's promised repair using his advice and decides not to give up the shop, so his work continues through her. Nothing in the story argues that old shops cannot compete.

questions.stem: According to the poem, how does the driver know the riders?
options: By the stops where they get on
By their names and their jobs
By the talks they have each night
By the fares they pay him
questions.explanation: The poem says "The driver knows each rider by the stop," and then names each rider by a stop. The riders "do not speak," so he has not learned about them by talking.

questions.stem: The tone of the poem is best described as:
questions.explanation: The poem notices small details about tired riders and calls the driver's extra second "his gift," which is gentle and caring. Nothing in it is angry, joking or afraid.

questions.stem: Why does the driver hold the doors "a second past the rule"?
options: To avoid being blamed when the bus runs late
To rest before the next stop
To give the riders the one kindness he can
To check whether riders have paid
questions.explanation: The poem calls the extra second "his gift, / the only one he has to give." Waiting for anyone who runs is a small kindness, not a way to protect himself.

questions.stem: In the poem, the bus is described as "a lit room rolling through a sleeping town" and "a small, warm room that waits for them." These images present the bus as:
options: a machine that ignores its riders
a symbol of the town's wealth
a crowded place no one wants to be
a shelter in the dark early hours
questions.explanation: A lit, warm room in a dark, sleeping town is a place of comfort and safety for the early riders. The poem never shows it as crowded or uncaring.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why do cities stay warm after sunset?
options: Pavement and roofs release stored heat slowly
Car engines and buses keep running late into the evening
Trees give off warm air at night
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says asphalt, concrete and dark roofs "absorb sunlight all day and release that heat slowly." Trees cool the air rather than warm it.

questions.stem: The author compares trees releasing water vapor to sweat cooling skin in order to:
options: argue that trees and people need the same amount of water
explain a process using something familiar
show that trees are similar to animals
questions.explanation: Most readers know how sweat cools the body, so the comparison makes the less familiar process of leaves cooling the air easy to picture.

questions.stem: Based on the passage, which plan is most likely to raise a city's tree canopy?
options: Planting only in the wealthiest areas
Planting as many seedlings as possible each spring
Planting trees and watering them for years
Replacing parks with shaded parking lots
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says many young trees die and that cities that succeed "pair planting with a plan for watering and care." Planting alone is called "the easy part."

questions.stem: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Cities are hotter than the countryside all year
Air conditioning is a better answer to urban heat than trees
Most street trees die within a few summers
Trees cool cities but need care and fair placement
questions.explanation: The passage explains how trees cool cities, then adds that young trees need care and that canopy is uneven across neighborhoods. The other choices pick out one detail or contradict it.

questions.stem: What does the author want the town council to do?
options: Vote against ending the evening hours
Close the library on slow mornings
Raise the library's budget by one percent
Move the evening hours to the weekend
questions.explanation: The editorial opens by calling the plan "a mistake" and says "the council should reject it." It does not ask for a budget increase or new weekend hours.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence most directly supports the claim that evenings are the library's busiest time?
options: The library stays open until 9 p.m. three nights
A third of visits come in a fifth of the hours
Many job seekers do not own a printer
The savings would be about one percent of the budget
questions.explanation: Getting nearly a third of visits in less than a fifth of the open hours means evenings are busier than average. The opening hours and the printer detail do not show how busy the evenings are.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the editorial states an opinion rather than a fact?
options: The savings are about one percent of the budget.
The library stays open until 9 p.m. three nights a week.
There are better places to find that money.
The town council will vote next month.
questions.explanation: Whether there are "better places" for the money is the author's judgment. The hours, the vote and the budget figure can all be checked.

questions.stem: How does the third paragraph mainly support the author's argument?
options: By giving the exact cost of keeping the evening hours
By answering the finance office's figures
By describing how the vote will work
By showing who would lose the most from the cut
questions.explanation: The paragraph lists who uses the library at night and ends by saying the cut "would hurt the residents with the fewest other options." The cost comes in the next paragraph.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did the Erie Canal connect?
options: The Hudson River and Lake Erie
Lake Erie and the Atlantic coast of Canada
New York City and the Mississippi River
questions.explanation: The first sentence says the channel would "connect the Hudson River to Lake Erie," running from Albany to Buffalo.

questions.stem: As it is used in the passage, the word "championed" most nearly means:
questions.explanation: Clinton's name was attached to the plan because he "championed" it, meaning he argued for it. Critics mocked the plan; he did not.

questions.stem: According to the passage, why did shipping costs fall after the canal opened?
options: Farmers moved closer to the East Coast
Railroads began to compete with the canal for freight
Boats could carry heavier loads cheaply
New roads were built beside the canal
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says canal boats "could carry far heavier loads for a fraction of the price" compared with wagons. Railroads came later and are not given as the reason.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage as a whole?
options: Critics of new projects are usually wrong
Railroads failed to replace the canal
Canals are still the cheapest way to ship goods
A public project can change a region's economy
questions.explanation: The final paragraph says the canal showed "a bold public project could reshape the economy of an entire region." The passage also says railroads took over most of the canal's freight.

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The subject is "Association," a single group, so it takes the singular verb "is planning." "Are," "were" and "have" are all plural forms here.

questions.stem: [2] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: The lot, for years, it has collected broken furniture, old tires and trash.
For years the lot has collected broken furniture, old tires and trash.
For years, collecting broken furniture, old tires and trash, the lot.
questions.explanation: One sentence with a list says the same thing without repeating "collected." The version starting "For years, collecting" has no main verb, and "The lot, for years, it" repeats the subject.

questions.stem: [3] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: sturdy shoes gloves, rakes and trash bags will be provided.
sturdy shoes, and gloves, rakes and trash bags will be provided.
sturdy shoes; gloves, rakes and trash bags will be provided.
questions.explanation: The draft joins two complete sentences with only a comma, a comma splice. A semicolon separates them. Adding "and" after the comma makes it sound as if volunteers wear gloves, rakes and bags.

questions.stem: [4] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "Courtesy of" is the standard phrase for something a business provides free. "On behalf of" means acting for someone, and "courteously by" and "in the courtesy of" are not idiomatic.

questions.stem: [5] Which choice is the best first sentence for paragraph 3?
options: The benefits would reach far beyond a tidy lot.
Rosa's Bakery has served the court for many years.
Some residents prefer flowers to vegetables.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 lists what a garden would give children, older residents and the block, so a sentence about the benefits introduces it. The building's age and the bakery are off topic.

questions.stem: [6] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: a chance for meeting there neighbors
a chance to meet their neighbors
a chance to meet they're neighbors
questions.explanation: The neighbors belong to the residents, so the possessive "their" is needed. "There" names a place and "they're" means "they are."

questions.stem: [7] The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the writer make this deletion?
options: No, because it adds another benefit of the garden
Yes, because it has nothing to do with the lot
No, because it explains how to sign up
Yes, because it only repeats the point about children
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 is about what the garden would do for residents, and feeling safer is one more benefit. The sentence does not repeat the point about children or explain signing up.

questions.stem: [8] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: If coming is your plan to do,
Being as you plan to come,
questions.explanation: "If you plan to come" says the same thing in five words. The draft is wordy, and "Being as" and "your plan to do" are awkward and nonstandard.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: Anyone who can lend a wheelbarrow would be
Anyone, who can lend a wheelbarrow would be
Anyone who can lend, a wheelbarrow would be
questions.explanation: A comma should not separate a subject ("Anyone who can lend a wheelbarrow") from its verb ("would be"). No comma is needed anywhere in this part.

questions.stem: [10] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: Thank you for helping your neighbors.
questions.explanation: A warm, plain thank-you fits a friendly letter to neighbors. "In conclusion" is stiff and unneeded, "Thanks a ton, folks!!" is too casual, and "We hereby extend" is too formal.

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The writer takes money from the sister, which is borrowing. "Lending" and "loaning" mean giving money out, and "owing" does not fit "from my sister."

questions.stem: [2] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: The results surprised me: I was spending more on takeout than on groceries.
The results surprised me I was spending more on takeout than on groceries.
The results surprised me, and spending more on takeout than on groceries.
questions.explanation: The draft is a comma splice. A colon works because the second part tells what the surprising result was. Leaving out all punctuation makes a run-on, and "and spending" leaves a fragment.

questions.stem: [3] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: Making a plan is the step after tracking spending, so "Next" shows the order. "However" and "Instead" signal a contrast, and "For example" signals an example.

questions.stem: [4] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "Won't" is the contraction of "will not," with the apostrophe where the letters were dropped. The other spellings put the apostrophe in the wrong place or leave it out.

questions.stem: [5] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: Twenty dollars, a week, does not sound like much money, to most.
To most people, twenty dollars a week is not a lot of money to them.
Twenty dollars a week may not sound like much.
questions.explanation: The short version keeps the meaning and cuts "to most people who hear about it." The version with three commas breaks up the sentence, and "to them" repeats "to most people."

questions.stem: [6] Which choice is the best first sentence for paragraph 4?
options: Sticking to the plan was not always easy.
Potluck dinners have a long history.
My sister also earns a weekly paycheck at her job.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 is about the hardest part of keeping to the budget, so a sentence about sticking to the plan introduces it. The sister's cooking, her paycheck and the history of potlucks wander from that point.

questions.stem: [7] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: they enjoyed it as much as mine.
they enjoyed it as much as I did.
they enjoyed it as much as myself.
questions.explanation: The sentence compares two people enjoying something, so the subject form is needed: "as much as I did." "Me" and "myself" are the wrong case, and "mine" is a possessive.

questions.stem: [8] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "Calmer," "less anxious" and "more relaxed" mean the same thing, so one word is enough. "More calmer" doubles the comparative.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: Having learned to track my spending, I grew more confident.
Having learned to track my spending, confidence grew in me.
My confidence grew, having learned to track my spending.
questions.explanation: The opening phrase describes the writer, so "I" must come right after it. In the draft and the versions with "confidence" as the subject, the confidence seems to have learned to track spending.

questions.stem: [10] Which choice keeps the tone of the essay and is the most direct?
options: If you are maybe kind of thinking about a budget, it would probably be good to write everything down.
Should a budget be contemplated, documentation of all expenditures is advised.
questions.explanation: The plain, friendly sentence matches the rest of the essay. "Maybe kind of" is wordy and unsure, "Budget starters: write!" is too clipped, and "documentation of all expenditures" is stiff.

questions.stem: What is $(3.2 \times 10^4)(2.5 \times 10^3)$ written in scientific notation?
questions.explanation: Multiply the numbers and add the exponents: $3.2 \times 2.5 = 8$ and $10^4 \times 10^3 = 10^7$. Multiplying the exponents gives $10^{12}$, and adding 3.2 and 2.5 gives 5.7.

questions.stem: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour to make 24 cookies. At the same rate, how many cups of flour are needed for 40 cookies?
questions.explanation: Each cookie uses $\frac{3}{24} = \frac{1}{8}$ cup, so 40 cookies use $\frac{40}{8} = 5$ cups. Adding the 16 extra cookies as 16 cups, or guessing from the difference, gives the wrong totals.

questions.stem: A jacket that costs \$80 is on sale for 25% off. A 5% sales tax is added to the sale price. What is the total cost?
questions.explanation: 25% off \$80 is \$80 - \$20 = \$60. Tax adds 5%: $60 \times 1.05 = 63$, so \$63. Taxing the full \$80 price gives \$84, and stopping at the sale price gives \$60.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is irrational?
questions.explanation: 50 is not a perfect square, so $\sqrt{50}$ cannot be written as a fraction of integers. $\sqrt{49} = 7$, 0.25 is $\frac{1}{4}$, and $\frac{7}{3}$ is already a fraction.

questions.stem: A 13-foot ladder leans against a wall. The bottom of the ladder is 5 feet from the wall. How high up the wall does the ladder reach?
questions.explanation: The ladder is the hypotenuse: $5^2 + h^2 = 13^2$, so $h^2 = 169 - 25 = 144$ and $h = 12$. Subtracting the lengths gives 8, and adding them gives 18.

questions.stem: A cylindrical can has a radius of 3 inches and a height of 10 inches. Using $V = \pi r^2 h$, what is its volume?
questions.explanation: $V = \pi \cdot 3^2 \cdot 10 = 90\pi$. Using $r$ instead of $r^2$ gives $30\pi$, using $2r$ gives $60\pi$, and squaring 30 gives $900\pi$.

questions.stem: Two angles are supplementary. Their measures are $5x$ degrees and $4x$ degrees. What is the measure of the larger angle?
questions.explanation: Supplementary angles add to 180: $9x = 180$, so $x = 20$. The larger angle is $5 \times 20 = 100$ degrees. The smaller is 80, and 20 is only the value of $x$.

questions.stem: A person 6 feet tall casts a shadow 4 feet long. At the same time, a tree casts a shadow 18 feet long. How tall is the tree?
questions.explanation: The triangles are similar, so height and shadow are in the same ratio: $\frac{6}{4} = \frac{h}{18}$, giving $h = 27$. Setting the ratio upside down gives 12.

questions.stem: Leah's first four quiz scores are 82, 90, 76 and 88. What score does she need on the fifth quiz for a mean of 85?
questions.explanation: A mean of 85 over five quizzes needs a total of $5 \times 85 = 425$. Her first four add to 336, so she needs $425 - 336 = 89$.

questions.stem: A bag holds 5 red, 3 blue and 2 green marbles. Two marbles are drawn without putting the first back. What is the probability that both are red?
questions.explanation: The first draw is red with probability $\frac{5}{10}$; then 4 of the 9 left are red. $\frac{5}{10} \times \frac{4}{9} = \frac{20}{90} = \frac{2}{9}$. Replacing the first marble would give $\frac{1}{4}$.

questions.stem:
A survey asked 200 commuters which they prefer.

| | Prefers bus | Prefers train | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Under 30 | 30 | 50 | 80 |
| 30 and over | 70 | 50 | 120 |
| Total | 100 | 100 | 200 |

What percent of commuters under 30 prefer the train?
questions.explanation: Of the 80 commuters under 30, 50 prefer the train: $\frac{50}{80} = 0.625$, or 62.5%. Dividing by all 200 commuters gives 25%, and 50 of the 100 train riders gives 50%.

questions.stem: The cost $y$, in dollars, of a taxi ride of $x$ miles is modeled by $y = 2.5x + 12$. What does 2.5 represent?
options: The cost of each additional mile
The total cost of a 12-mile ride
The cost of the ride before any miles
The number of miles in a typical ride
questions.explanation: In $y = mx + b$, the slope $m$ is the change in cost per mile, so each mile adds \$2.50. The 12 is the starting charge before any miles are driven.

questions.stem: What value of $x$ makes $4(x - 3) = 2x + 10$ true?
questions.explanation: Distribute: $4x - 12 = 2x + 10$. Subtract $2x$ and add 12: $2x = 22$, so $x = 11$. Forgetting to multiply the 3 by 4 gives 6.5, and stopping at $2x = 22$ gives 22.

questions.stem: If $x + y = 12$ and $x - y = 4$, what is the value of $y$?
questions.explanation: Add the equations: $2x = 16$, so $x = 8$. Then $8 + y = 12$ gives $y = 4$. 8 is the value of $x$, not $y$.

questions.stem: What are the solutions of $x^2 - 5x - 14 = 0$?
questions.explanation: Find two numbers that multiply to $-14$ and add to $-5$: $-7$ and $2$. So $(x - 7)(x + 2) = 0$, giving $x = 7$ or $x = -2$. Flipping the signs of the factors gives the wrong solutions.

questions.stem: Which inequality is the solution of $3x - 7 > 11$?
questions.explanation: Add 7: $3x > 18$. Divide by 3: $x > 6$. The sign flips only when dividing by a negative number, so it stays $>$. Subtracting 7 instead of adding gives $\frac{4}{3}$.
$f(-2) = 2(4) - 3(-2) + 1 = 8 + 6 + 1 = 15$. Dropping the negative on $-3(-2)$ gives 3, and squaring $2x$ instead of $x$ gives 23.

questions.stem: What is the slope of the line through the points $(-1, 4)$ and $(3, -8)$?
questions.explanation: Slope is $\frac{-8 - 4}{3 - (-1)} = \frac{-12}{4} = -3$. Losing the negative sign gives 3, using only 3 as the run gives $-4$, and using only $-8$ as the rise gives $-2$.

questions.stem: The formula $A = P + Prt$ gives the amount $A$ in an account with simple interest. Which equation is solved for $r$?
questions.explanation: Subtract $P$ from both sides: $A - P = Prt$. Then divide by $Pt$: $r = \frac{A - P}{Pt}$. Dividing by $t$ alone leaves a $P$ on the right.

questions.stem: A town's population of 2,000 doubles every 5 years. What will the population be after 15 years?
questions.explanation: 15 years is three doubling periods: $2{,}000 \times 2^3 = 16{,}000$. Tripling gives 6,000, and four doublings gives 32,000.

questions.stem: A gym charges a \$40 sign-up fee and \$25 a month. Which equation gives the total cost $C$ after $m$ months?
questions.explanation: The monthly charge multiplies the number of months and the one-time fee is added once: $C = 25m + 40$. Swapping the numbers charges the fee every month.

questions.stem: What value of $x$ makes $\sqrt{x + 5} = 4$ true?
questions.explanation: Square both sides: $x + 5 = 16$, so $x = 11$. Check: $\sqrt{16} = 4$. Subtracting 5 from 4 before squaring gives $-1$, and adding 5 to 16 gives 21.

questions.stem: What is the independent variable in the student's investigation?
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the student changed on purpose, the color of the light. Height is what was measured (the dependent variable), and water and days were kept the same.

questions.stem: Why did the student give every seedling the same water, soil and temperature?
options: So that the green-light plants would survive
So that only the light color could cause the differences
So that the seedlings would grow as tall as possible
So that the seedlings would need less light each day to grow
questions.explanation: Keeping everything else the same means any difference in height can be traced to the one thing that changed, the light color.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the results?
options: Light color has no effect on growth
Seedlings need red light to grow at all
Seedlings grow poorly under green light
Blue light makes seedlings grow twice as tall as white
questions.explanation: Green-light seedlings averaged 6.2 cm, less than half of every other group. Red-light seedlings did grow, and blue (14.1 cm) is only slightly taller than white (13.5 cm).

questions.stem: At which temperature was catalase most active?
questions.explanation: The most bubbles, 31 per minute, were counted at 40°C. Activity rose up to 40°C and then fell.

questions.stem: Which best explains why activity was so low at 60°C?
options: Heat changed the enzyme's shape so it worked poorly
The potato extract contained no catalase at 60°C
Enzymes work faster as temperature keeps rising
The hydrogen peroxide had all been used up before the test
questions.explanation: Enzymes are proteins whose shape lets them work. Too much heat changes (denatures) that shape, so activity drops. The same extract was used at every temperature.

questions.stem: The class wants to find the best temperature more exactly. Which next step makes the most sense?
options: Count bubbles for ten seconds instead of a minute
Test temperatures between 30°C and 50°C in small steps
Use a different enzyme at the same six temperatures
Repeat the whole test at 10°C several more times to check it
questions.explanation: The peak lies somewhere between 30°C and 50°C, so testing closely spaced temperatures in that range would locate it. A shorter count or a new enzyme would not answer the question.

questions.stem: Which cell structure controls what enters and leaves the cell?
questions.explanation: The cell membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances through and keeps others out. The nucleus holds DNA, ribosomes make proteins, and the cell wall gives plant cells support.

questions.stem: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones, which protect them from predators. The clownfish chase away fish that eat anemones. What kind of relationship is this?
questions.explanation: Both species benefit, which is mutualism. In parasitism one organism is harmed, in predation one eats the other, and in competition both are harmed by sharing a resource.

questions.stem: In pea plants, the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant over the allele for white flowers (p). Two plants with the genotype Pp are crossed. What fraction of their offspring is expected to have white flowers?
questions.explanation: A Punnett square for Pp x Pp gives PP, Pp, Pp and pp. Only pp shows the recessive white color, one out of four. Three of four are purple.

questions.stem: Which substances does a plant use to make sugar during photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: Using light energy, plants combine carbon dioxide and water to make sugar, releasing oxygen. Oxygen and sugar are the products, not the starting materials.

questions.stem: On which surface did the car roll the shortest distance?
questions.explanation: The car rolled only 30 cm on sandpaper, the least of the four surfaces.

questions.stem: Which best explains the different distances in the results?
options: Smoother surfaces push the car forward
The car carried more weight when it rolled on rough surfaces
The ramp was steeper for the tile trial
Rougher surfaces cause more friction, which slows the car
questions.explanation: Friction opposes motion, and rough surfaces like sandpaper and carpet produce more of it, so the car stops sooner. The same car and ramp were used every time.

questions.stem: A block has a mass of 60 grams and a volume of 20 cubic centimeters. What is its density?
questions.explanation: Density is mass divided by volume: $60 \div 20 = 3$ g/cm³. Dividing the other way gives 0.33, and multiplying gives 1,200.

questions.stem: The same push is given to an empty shopping cart and to a full one. Which statement is true?
options: The empty cart speeds up more
Both carts speed up the same amount
The full cart speeds up more
questions.explanation: By Newton's second law, acceleration equals force divided by mass. With the same force, the smaller mass, the empty cart, accelerates more.

questions.stem: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.explanation: Rusting forms a new substance, iron oxide. Melting, dissolving and breaking change the form of a substance but not what it is made of.

questions.stem: On which day was the air pressure lowest?
questions.explanation: Thursday's reading, 997 millibars, is the lowest in the table.

questions.stem: Which pattern do the data support?
options: High pressure came before heavy rain
Pressure rose each day as the weather slowly cleared up
Air pressure stayed the same all week
Falling pressure came before cloudier, wetter weather
questions.explanation: Pressure fell from 1022 to 997 millibars as the weather went from clear to heavy rain, then rose on Friday as it cleared. Low pressure is linked to clouds and storms.

questions.skill: Earth's position in the solar system
questions.stem: What is the main reason Earth has seasons?
options: The Sun gives off more energy in summer
Earth is closer to the Sun in summer
questions.explanation: Because Earth's axis is tilted, each hemisphere gets more direct sunlight for part of the year. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during the Northern Hemisphere's winter.

questions.stem: How do sedimentary rocks such as sandstone usually form?
options: Heat and pressure change existing rock deep underground
Layers of sediment are pressed and cemented together
Melted rock cools and hardens below the surface
Lava cools quickly at the surface
questions.explanation: Sediment such as sand settles in layers that are compacted and cemented over time. Cooling melted rock forms igneous rock, and heat and pressure form metamorphic rock.

questions.stem: A star like the Sun has used up the hydrogen in its core. What will it most likely become next?
questions.explanation: When a Sun-like star runs out of core hydrogen, it swells into a red giant before shedding its outer layers and leaving a white dwarf. Black holes and neutron stars form from much more massive stars.

questions.stem: According to the excerpt, where does a government get its just powers?
options: From the consent of the people it governs
From the wealth and property of its richest leaders
From the strength of its army
From the king who rules it
questions.explanation: The excerpt says governments derive "their just powers from the consent of the governed," meaning from the people themselves.

questions.stem: The ideas in this excerpt were mainly used to:
options: set up the first U.S. Congress
end slavery in the United States
questions.explanation: The Declaration argued that people may change a government that fails to protect their rights, which supported independence from Britain. It did not create Congress or end slavery.

questions.skill: The Great Depression and New Deal
questions.stem: Which New Deal program, created in 1935, still provides monthly payments to retired workers?
questions.explanation: The Social Security Act of 1935 set up old-age insurance for retired workers. Medicare began in 1965, the Peace Corps in 1961, and the Federal Reserve in 1913.

questions.stem: Which amendment, ratified in 1865, abolished slavery in the United States?
questions.explanation: The Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery. The Fifteenth protected voting regardless of race, and the Nineteenth protected women's right to vote.

questions.stem: During the Cold War, the U.S. policy of containment aimed to:
options: take over the Soviet Union and its allies
questions.explanation: Containment meant keeping communism from expanding beyond where it already was, through aid, alliances and, at times, military action. It did not aim to conquer the Soviet Union.

questions.stem: Why did ancient Egyptian civilization grow up along the Nile River?
options: The river was the only source of gold
Yearly floods left rich soil for farming
The desert around it had plenty of rain
The river protected it from all invaders
questions.explanation: Each year the Nile flooded and left fertile silt behind, so farmers could grow enough food to support cities. The land beyond the river was dry desert.

questions.stem: The exchange of plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and Europe after 1492 is called:
questions.explanation: The Columbian Exchange brought crops such as corn and potatoes to Europe and horses, wheat and diseases such as smallpox to the Americas. The Silk Road was an older trade route across Asia.

questions.stem: Which right is protected by the First Amendment?
options: The right to a jury trial
questions.explanation: The excerpt names freedom of the press along with religion, speech, assembly and petition. Jury trials, arms and searches are in other amendments.

questions.stem: A group of residents signs a letter asking the city to fix a dangerous intersection. Which First Amendment right are they using?
options: The right to petition the government
The free exercise of religion in public
questions.explanation: Asking the government to correct a problem is petitioning "for a redress of grievances." The right to remain silent comes from the Fifth Amendment.

questions.stem: The president vetoes a bill passed by Congress. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: A veto lets the executive branch check the legislative branch. Judicial review is the courts' power to strike down laws, and federalism divides power between national and state governments.

questions.stem: Under the Tenth Amendment, powers not given to the federal government and not denied to the states belong to:
questions.explanation: The Tenth Amendment reserves those powers "to the States respectively, or to the people." This is the basis of many state powers, such as running schools.

questions.stem: How many senators does each state have in the U.S. Senate?
questions.explanation: The Constitution gives every state two senators. Seats in the House of Representatives, not the Senate, depend on population.

questions.stem: In a parliamentary system, the head of government, often called the prime minister, is usually:
options: picked by the party with the most seats
the oldest member of the royal family
elected directly by the people for a fixed term
questions.explanation: In a parliamentary system the leader comes from the majority in parliament and depends on its support. In the U.S. presidential system, the president is elected separately from Congress.

questions.stem: Which is a responsibility, not just a right, of U.S. citizens?
options: Serving on a jury when called
questions.explanation: Citizens are required to serve on a jury when summoned. Choosing a religion, free speech and travel are rights people may use or not.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the pattern in the table?
options: The price fell a little every week
The number sold did not depend on price
As the price rose, fewer quarts were sold
As the price rose, more quarts were sold each week
questions.explanation: Sales fell from 300 quarts at the lowest price to 150 at the highest. This matches the law of demand: higher prices lead buyers to purchase less.

questions.stem: In which week did the market earn the most money from strawberries?
questions.explanation: Multiply price by quarts sold: June 1 brought in \$1,200, June 8 \$1,250, June 15 \$1,140 and June 22 \$1,050. The highest price did not bring in the most money, because sales fell.

questions.stem: Mia can spend Saturday working a shift that pays well or going to a concert. She chooses the concert. What is her opportunity cost?
options: The pay she gave up by not working
The money she will earn next week
The price of the concert ticket
The two hours she spent at the concert
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the best choice given up. By going to the concert, Mia gives up the pay from her shift.

questions.stem: Two savings accounts pay the same interest rate. One pays simple interest and the other compound interest. Over many years, which is true?
options: The simple account grows more, because it is safer
The compound account, since interest earns interest
Both accounts grow by exactly the same amount
Neither account grows unless money is added
questions.explanation: Compound interest is paid on the balance, including past interest, so the account grows faster each year. Simple interest is paid only on the original deposit.

questions.stem: A country's population pyramid is very wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. What does this most likely show?
options: An aging population that is slowly shrinking
A population with many more men than women
A young population that is growing quickly
A population that is not changing
questions.explanation: A wide base means many children compared with older people, the sign of high birth rates and a growing population. An aging country has a narrower base.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a push factor that leads people to leave a region?
options: A city with many new jobs
A town with low housing costs and rents
A long drought that ruins farms
questions.explanation: Push factors drive people away from a place, such as drought, war or lack of work. Jobs, schools and cheap housing are pull factors that draw people to a place.

questions.stem: Why is Marisol surprised to see her grandmother at the diner?
options: Her grandmother never eats in restaurants
Her grandmother had said she disliked Marisol's job
Her grandmother lives in another town
Her grandmother had been ill for weeks
questions.explanation: The story says "Abuela never ate in restaurants" and quotes her saying it is a waste to pay someone to cook worse than you.

questions.stem: Marisol's sudden awareness of the grease spot and her loose ponytail suggests that she:
options: wants to make a good impression
plans to quit the job soon
has been working too many hours
questions.explanation: Noticing small flaws in her appearance just as her grandmother sits down shows she cares how she looks to her. Nothing suggests shame or plans to quit.

questions.stem: The note says, "THE EGGS WERE NOT BAD. YOU STOOD UP STRAIGHT." What does this suggest about the grandmother?
options: She was unhappy with the meal
She wants Marisol to cook instead
She shows pride in a reserved way
She did not notice Marisol at work
questions.explanation: "Not bad" is high praise from someone who distrusts restaurant food, and the comment on posture shows she was watching Marisol with pride. She expresses it briefly, in writing.

questions.stem: The detail that the note "stayed for the rest of the summer" in Marisol's pocket mainly shows that:
options: she planned to show the note to Lou at the grill
she forgot the note was there
she needed to save the money
the approval mattered a great deal to her
questions.explanation: Keeping the note close all summer shows how much her grandmother's few words meant to her. The money is separate from the note.

questions.stem: What does the mother do in the garden in February?
options: Names the crops she will plant
Measures the snow on the rows
Pulls up the broken stalks from last year
questions.explanation: She "names what isn't there": the beans, squash and onions she plans for summer. The speaker sees only mud and broken stalks.

questions.stem: The poem contrasts the speaker and the mother mainly by showing that:
options: the mother works and the speaker only watches
the speaker sees what is, the mother what will be
the speaker loves gardening much more than the mother
the mother has forgotten last summer's harvest
questions.explanation: "I see a field of mud" is set against "She sees July." One sees what is there now, the other what the garden will become.

questions.stem: What does the line "how hope is just a kind of careful math" suggest?
options: Gardening needs a strong head for numbers
Hope cannot be measured or counted
Hope comes from planning, not only wishing
The mother worries about the cost of seeds
questions.explanation: The mother counts rows and studies seed packets; her hope for July rests on that careful planning. The line is not about arithmetic skill or money.

questions.stem: How does the speaker's attitude change over the course of the poem?
options: From quiet hope to bitter disappointment
questions.explanation: "I used to laugh" marks the speaker's earlier doubt; "Now I am learning how she reads the ground" shows a new understanding of the mother's view.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how did DDT harm bald eagles?
options: It made their eggshells too thin
It killed the fish they ate
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says DDT "did not usually kill adult birds" but caused eggs with shells so thin they cracked.

questions.stem: Which event happened first, according to the passage?
options: Most uses of DDT were banned
Nesting pairs fell below 500 in the lower 48
The eagle was removed from the endangered list
Biologists released chicks in new areas
questions.explanation: The decline to fewer than 500 pairs is placed in the early 1960s, before the 1972 ban, the releases and the 2007 delisting.

questions.stem: Which statement about DDT can be inferred from the passage?
options: It was banned because it failed to kill enough insects
It was used mainly to kill eagles
Its effects could travel through a food chain
It stopped working on insects by 1972
questions.explanation: DDT moved from water into fish and then into eagles that ate them, harming birds that were never sprayed. The passage gives no other reason for the ban.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the final paragraph?
options: To predict that eagles will decline again
To describe how the ban was passed
To compare eagles with other endangered birds
To state the broader lessons of the recovery
questions.explanation: The last paragraph steps back from the eagle's story to draw two general lessons about science, policy and chemical harm.

questions.stem: Which change will the health center make on Fridays?
options: It will close at 5 p.m. instead of 7 p.m.
It will be open only for children
It will open at 9 a.m. instead of 8 a.m. on Fridays
It will stop taking walk-in visits
questions.explanation: The letter says that to make the new hours possible, the center "will close at 5 p.m. on Fridays instead of 7 p.m."

questions.stem: Why does the letter mention the patient survey?
options: To ask patients to fill out a new survey
To show that the changes answer patients' requests
To explain why the center is cutting staff and hours
To report complaints about walk-in visits
questions.explanation: The letter says "These changes come from you" and gives the most common survey requests, early and weekend appointments.

questions.stem: Why does the center encourage patients to book Saturday visits ahead?
options: It will no longer accept walk-in visits on weekdays
Saturday visits cost more than others
It expects Saturday times to fill quickly
It has fewer doctors during the week
questions.explanation: The letter says Saturday is a day "which we expect to fill quickly." Walk-ins remain available on weekday mornings.

questions.stem: The request to tell family members who do not use the portal suggests the center wants to:
options: close its front desk phone line
limit visits to one family member
move all booking to the patient portal next year
reach patients who may miss online notices
questions.explanation: Asking readers to pass the news on shows concern for patients who would not see a message posted online.

questions.stem: According to Passage 1, why has the district found it easier to hire teachers?
options: Teachers see the schedule as a benefit
Teachers work fewer hours in total each week
questions.explanation: The parent writes that the district has had an easier time hiring teachers, "who see the schedule as a benefit." Pay and class size are not mentioned.

questions.stem: On which point do the two passages agree?
options: Test scores rise in every district with a four-day week
The four-day week can save districts money
The fifth day is hard on every family
questions.explanation: Passage 1 says the district saved money on buses and heating, and Passage 2 says districts report "modest savings." They disagree about learning and families.

questions.stem: How does the author of Passage 2 mainly differ from the author of Passage 1?
options: By arguing that savings are too small
By sharing a personal family experience
By weighing research and effects on others
By supporting the four-day week without doubts
questions.explanation: Passage 1 rests on one family's experience; Passage 2 draws on studies and asks about working parents and students who rely on school meals.

questions.stem: Based on Passage 2, the researcher would most likely want the parent in Passage 1 to consider:
options: the cost of heating school buildings
how teachers feel about the schedule
the time families spend at medical appointments
families who lack care on the fifth day
questions.explanation: The researcher warns that the fifth day can leave some families without care or meals, a group the parent, whose family benefits, does not mention.

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The championship belongs to the team, so the possessive "its" is needed, with no apostrophe. "It's" means "it is."

questions.stem: [2] The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the writer make this deletion?
options: Yes, because it only repeats what the first paragraph says
No, because it tells when and how the project started
Yes, because it is not about robotics
No, because it names the team captain
questions.explanation: The sentence opens the paragraph about how the project began and leads into Reyes's account of where the idea came from. Nothing else gives the start date.

questions.stem: [3] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "That" refers to "something," which is singular, so the verb is "looks." "Look" and "have looked" are plural forms, and "looking" cannot be the main verb.

questions.stem: [4] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The article tells about the past ("was harder"), so the expectation is past too: "expected." The present and future forms do not fit.

questions.stem: [5] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: The students rebuilt the gripper four times. They tested. Each version was tested for hours
Four times rebuilt by the students, the gripper, testing each version for hours
The gripper was rebuilt, and the gripper was tested, four times by the students for hours
questions.explanation: The draft is clear and uses a phrase to add the testing detail. Breaking it into three short sentences is choppy and repeats "tested," "Four times rebuilt" has no main verb, and the last version repeats "the gripper."

questions.stem: [6] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: Their coach, Mr. Dale who teaches physics he stayed late
Their coach, Mr. Dale, who teaches physics, stayed late
Their coach Mr. Dale, who teaches physics he, stayed late
questions.explanation: The subject "Their coach" already has its verb "stayed," so the extra "he" must go. The phrases that describe the coach are set off by commas.

questions.stem: [7] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The paragraph moves from the struggles to the result, so "In the end" fits. "Furthermore" adds a point, "Similarly" compares, and "For instance" gives an example.

questions.stem: [8] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: "The robot's speed and its accuracy" pairs two nouns. The draft breaks the pattern with a clause, and "accurate and also correct" repeats the idea.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: The team will now go on to compete in May at the state level of competition.
The team will now compete at the state level in May.
In May, the team will now go on, at the state level, competing.
questions.explanation: "Compete at the state level in May" keeps every fact and drops "go on to," "of competition" and "the month of." The other versions stay wordy or scramble the sentence.

questions.stem: [10] The writer wants to end the article with a detail that shows Reyes's sense of humor. Which choice best does this?
options: The team meets every Tuesday after school.
Robots are used in many recycling plants.
The robot weighs about forty pounds.
questions.explanation: The joke about convincing the principal to let them plug it in shows Reyes's humor and ties back to the cafeteria. The meeting day, recycling plants and the robot's weight are plain facts.

questions.stem: [1] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The position was advertised on the website, so the past participle "advertised" is right. "Adverted" means referred to, a different word.

questions.stem: [2] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: totally know I would crush it on your team
reckon I am fit for your team
believe me when I say I am the best ever
questions.explanation: A cover letter needs a confident, polite tone, which the draft has. "Crush it" and "reckon" are slang, and "the best ever" is boastful.

questions.stem: [3] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: In my current job at Daily Market, I train new cashiers also, I manage the schedule
In my current job at Daily Market I train new cashiers I also manage the schedule
In my current job at Daily Market, I train new cashiers and also manage the schedule
questions.explanation: The draft joins two sentences with only a comma. Joining the two verbs with "and" fixes it. Moving "also" keeps the comma splice, and dropping the comma makes a run-on.

questions.stem: [4] The writer is considering deleting the underlined sentence. Should the writer make this deletion?
options: Yes, because it is unrelated to the job
Yes, because it repeats the second paragraph
No, because it shows the result of the writer's idea
No, because it explains the new restocking method in detail
questions.explanation: Saying the change cut overtime costs shows a manager what the writer's suggestion achieved, strong support for the application.

questions.stem: [5] Which choice is the best first sentence for paragraph 3?
options: I am also good with people under pressure.
Daily Market is open until midnight.
I live only a short drive from your Greenway store.
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 describes helping customers and staying calm when busy, so a sentence about working well with people introduces it. Food, distance and store hours have no place there.

questions.stem: [6] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: I try to solve it fast quickly
I try to solve it quickly
I try quickly and fast to solve it
questions.explanation: "Fast" and "quick" mean the same thing, and "quickly" is the adverb that describes how the writer solves problems.

questions.stem: [7] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: This job is a job I would like to talk about.
Talking about the job, more, I would welcome.
I would welcome, the chance to talk with you, more.
questions.explanation: The draft is clear and polite. The other versions repeat "job," scramble the word order, or add commas that break up the sentence.

questions.stem: [8] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject, so it takes the subject form "I," and courtesy puts the other person first. "Me" and "myself" are not used as subjects.

questions.stem: [9] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
questions.explanation: The subject of both verbs is "I" ("I can be reached ... and am available"), so "am" is correct.

questions.stem: [10] Which choice is best for the underlined portion?
options: Thank you for your time and consideration.
Your time is something I thank you for, a lot.
questions.explanation: A short, formal thank-you suits a letter to a hiring manager. The draft is slang and a comma splice, "Thx" is too casual, and "something I thank you for, a lot" is awkward.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to $(2x^3)^2$?
questions.explanation: Square both factors: $2^2 = 4$ and $(x^3)^2 = x^6$. Forgetting to square the 2 gives $2x^6$, and adding the exponents gives $x^5$.

questions.stem: A driver travels 150 miles in 2.5 hours. What is the average speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is distance divided by time: $\frac{150}{2.5} = 60$. Multiplying instead gives 375.

questions.stem: The price of a meal rose from \$40 to \$50. By what percent did the price increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 10 on a starting price of 40: $\frac{10}{40} = 0.25$, or 25%. Dividing by the new price, 50, gives 20%.

questions.stem: Which expression has a rational value?
questions.explanation: $\sqrt{8} \cdot \sqrt{2} = \sqrt{16} = 4$, a whole number. $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}$, which is still irrational, as are $\pi + 1$ and $\sqrt{3}$.

questions.stem: What is the distance between the points $(1, 2)$ and $(7, 10)$?
questions.explanation: The horizontal change is 6 and the vertical change is 8. By the Pythagorean Theorem, $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = \sqrt{100} = 10$. Adding 6 and 8 gives 14, and forgetting the square root gives 100.

questions.stem: A circular rug has a diameter of 10 feet. Using $A = \pi r^2$, what is its area?
questions.explanation: The radius is half the diameter, 5 feet: $A = \pi \cdot 5^2 = 25\pi$. Using the diameter as the radius gives $100\pi$, and $10\pi$ is the circumference.

questions.stem: A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 centimeters is dilated by a scale factor of 2.5. How long is the longest side of the new triangle?
questions.explanation: A dilation multiplies every length by the scale factor: $5 \times 2.5 = 12.5$. 7.5 and 10 are the other two new sides.

questions.stem: A town of 45,000 people covers 18 square miles. What is its population density?
questions.explanation: Density is people divided by area: $\frac{45{,}000}{18} = 2{,}500$. Multiplying instead gives 810,000.

questions.stem: What is the median of the data set 4, 9, 22, 17, 11, 20?
questions.explanation: In order: 4, 9, 11, 17, 20, 22. With six values, the median is the mean of the middle two: $\frac{11 + 17}{2} = 14$. 18 is the range.

questions.stem: A box plot of commute times, in minutes, has a minimum of 10, a first quartile of 18, a median of 25, a third quartile of 34 and a maximum of 60. What is the interquartile range?
questions.explanation: The interquartile range is the third quartile minus the first: $34 - 18 = 16$. The range is $60 - 10 = 50$, and 25 is the median.

questions.stem: A principal wants a random sample of 50 students to survey about lunch. Which method is best?
options: Have a computer pick 50 names from the full enrollment list
Ask the first 50 students in the lunch line
Ask for 50 volunteers over the loudspeaker
Survey the 50 students on the student council
questions.explanation: A random sample gives every student the same chance of being chosen. Students in the lunch line, on the council or who volunteer are groups that may think differently from the rest.

questions.stem: A coin is tossed and a spinner with four equal sections numbered 1 to 4 is spun. What is the probability of heads and a 3?
questions.explanation: The events are independent, so multiply: $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{8}$. Adding the probabilities gives $\frac{3}{4}$.

questions.stem: What value of $x$ makes $\frac{x}{3} + 5 = 9$ true?
questions.explanation: Subtract 5: $\frac{x}{3} = 4$. Multiply by 3: $x = 12$. Stopping at 4 forgets the division by 3, and multiplying 14 by 3 gives 42.

questions.stem: A theater sold 50 tickets for \$475. Adult tickets cost \$12 and child tickets cost \$7. How many adult tickets were sold?
What are the solutions of $x^2 - 6x + 4 = 0$?
questions.explanation: $x = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{36 - 16}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm \sqrt{20}}{2} = \frac{6 \pm 2\sqrt{5}}{2} = 3 \pm \sqrt{5}$. Using $-b$ as $-6$ gives $-3$, and adding $36 + 16$ gives $\sqrt{13}$.
Subtract each term: $3x^2 - x^2 = 2x^2$, $2x - (-4x) = 6x$, and $-5 - 1 = -6$. Not distributing the minus sign gives $-2x$ and $-4$.

questions.stem: How many solutions does the system $y = 2x + 3$ and $4x - 2y = 6$ have?
questions.explanation: Solving the second equation for $y$ gives $y = 2x - 3$. Both lines have slope 2 but different $y$-intercepts, so they are parallel and never meet.

questions.stem: A town's population was 1,200 in 2018, 1,560 in 2021 and 2,100 in 2024. What was the average rate of change from 2018 to 2024?
questions.explanation: Change in population over change in time: $\frac{2{,}100 - 1{,}200}{2024 - 2018} = \frac{900}{6} = 150$. 120 is the rate for 2018 to 2021 only, and 900 forgets to divide by the years.

questions.stem: The function $f(n)$ gives the cost of buying $n$ concert tickets. Each customer must buy at least 1 ticket and may buy at most 8. What is the domain of $f$?
questions.explanation: Tickets come in whole numbers, and the limits are 1 and 8, so the domain is 1, 2, 3, ... 8. Real numbers would include fractions of a ticket, and 0 tickets is not allowed.

questions.stem: A monthly electric bill is $C = 0.12k + 15$, where $k$ is the kilowatt-hours used. What does 15 represent?
options: A charge paid even if no electricity is used
questions.explanation: When $k = 0$, $C = 15$, so 15 is a fixed monthly charge. 0.12 is the price of each kilowatt-hour.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the function $y = 500(1.04)^t$?
questions.explanation: A factor of 1.04 keeps 100% of the amount and adds 4% each period. Growth of 104% would need a factor of 2.04, and a factor below 1 would mean shrinking.

questions.stem: What are the solutions of $|2x - 5| = 9$?
questions.explanation: Either $2x - 5 = 9$, so $x = 7$, or $2x - 5 = -9$, so $x = -2$. Forgetting the negative case gives only 7.

questions.stem: In which year was the wolf population largest?
questions.explanation: The table shows 38 wolves in Year 5, more than in any other year.

questions.stem: Which best explains why the moose population fell between Year 3 and Year 7?
options: The growing wolf population ate more moose
The moose ran out of predators
Moose moved to the wolves' side of the island
Fewer wolves left more food for moose
questions.explanation: Wolves increased to 38 by Year 5, and more predators eat more prey, so moose dropped from 1,600 to 700. The island is isolated, so the moose could not leave.

questions.stem: Based on the pattern, what is most likely to happen to the wolves a few years after Year 9?
options: Their numbers will keep falling forever
Their numbers will rise as the moose recover
They will die out completely within a few years
questions.explanation: Moose were rising again by Year 9 after the wolves declined. More prey means more food for wolves, so the wolf count is likely to climb again, continuing the cycle.

questions.stem: What did the student change on purpose in this investigation?
questions.explanation: Only the sugar was varied, from 0 to 20 grams. The yeast and water were the same in each bottle, and the balloon size was the result measured.

questions.stem: What was the purpose of the bottle with no sugar?
options: To make the experiment finish faster
To keep the other bottles warm
To give the yeast in that bottle more room to grow
To show whether yeast makes gas without sugar
questions.explanation: The no-sugar bottle is the control. Its flat balloon shows that the gas in the other bottles came from the yeast breaking down sugar.

questions.stem: Which conclusion do the results best support?
options: More sugar led to more carbon dioxide
Yeast works best with exactly 10 grams of sugar
Balloon size does not depend on sugar
Sugar stops yeast from making gas
questions.explanation: Balloon size grew with each increase in sugar, from 14 cm at 5 g to 31 cm at 20 g, showing more carbon dioxide was released.

questions.stem: Which cell structure releases most of the energy a cell gets from food?
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, releasing energy from sugar. Chloroplasts capture light energy in plants, and vacuoles store water and other materials.

questions.stem: Which type of molecule is the body's main source of quick energy?
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates such as glucose are broken down first for energy. Proteins mainly build and repair tissue, and nucleic acids such as DNA carry genetic information.

questions.stem: On a hot day, a person sweats. What does sweating do for the body?
options: It warms the body by trapping heat near the skin
It adds water to the blood
It cools the body as the sweat evaporates
questions.explanation: Evaporating sweat carries heat away from the skin, helping keep body temperature steady. This is one way the body maintains homeostasis.

questions.stem: A change in the sequence of a gene's DNA is called:
questions.explanation: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. A chromosome is a long strand of DNA, an allele is one version of a gene, and a trait is a feature such as eye color.

questions.stem: About how much sugar dissolves in 100 g of water at 40°C?
questions.explanation: The table gives 238 g of sugar at 40°C. 36.4 g is the figure for table salt at the same temperature.

questions.stem: Which statement is supported by the table?
options: Salt dissolves twice as well at 80°C as at 0°C
Heat raises sugar's solubility far more than salt's
Salt dissolves better than sugar at every temperature
Neither substance dissolves better in warm water
questions.explanation: From 0°C to 80°C, sugar rises from 179 g to 362 g, but salt only from 35.7 g to 38.0 g. Both dissolve a little better in warmer water.

questions.stem: A wire is wrapped around an iron nail and connected to a battery. The nail can now pick up paper clips. Why?
options: The wire is made of a magnetic metal
The heat from the battery magnetizes the iron nail
The electric current creates a magnetic field
The paper clips carry an electric charge
